title: Recovering Repressed Memories
summary: The controversy over repressed and recovered memories, and three unusual memory phenomena: flashbulb memories, their features, and eidetic imagery.

lesson.title: Can the mind bury a memory?
lesson.hook: Nollywood loves the scene: a grown woman suddenly 'remembers' a childhood horror that explains everything wrong in her life. Psychologists have fought bitterly over whether real memory works like that.

slides.heading: What repression means
slides.body:
**Repression** is the idea that when a thought, feeling or memory is too painful to bear, the mind **unconsciously** pushes it out of awareness. The person is not choosing to forget; they simply become unaware the memory exists.

The concept comes from **Sigmund Freud**, who saw repression as a central **defence mechanism** protecting the ego from anxiety. The key word is *unconscious*: deliberately trying not to think about something is suppression, not repression.

slides.heading: Repressed and recovered memory
slides.body:
The fuller claim goes like this. A **trauma** is so severe that it cannot stay in conscious memory, so it is removed by **repression**, **dissociation** (a split between the experience and normal awareness), or both.

Years later the memory may return, often in an ordinary, harmless setting, such as a smell or a film scene, and reappear in consciousness. This returning memory is called a **recovered memory**.

slides.question: Which feature most clearly separates repression from simply trying not to think about something?
options: Repression involves a pleasant memory
Repression happens unconsciously
Repression always takes place in adulthood
Repression improves recall of the event
slides.why: Repression is an unconscious process; deliberately pushing a thought away is suppression. Repressed material is painful, not pleasant.

slides.heading: How the idea spread
slides.body:
Many people believe that buried memories of childhood abuse can cause serious problems in adult life (Stafford and Lynn, 2002). Films, novels and television have spread this belief.

Self-help books pushed it further. The best known is ***The Courage to Heal*** (1988) by **Ellen Bass and Laura Davis**. It became a 'bible' for abuse survivors and a main text for some therapists who treated them.

slides.heading: The controversial advice
slides.body:
Bass and Davis did not only help people who remembered abuse. They also reached out to people with **no memory** of abuse at all.

Their message, in summary: if you have a feeling something abusive happened, it probably did; if you suspect abuse and have the 'symptoms', you were abused; and you do **not need proof**.

Notice the problem. A feeling, plus vague symptoms that almost anyone has, was treated as enough to conclude that abuse happened.

slides.heading: Why psychologists are sceptical
slides.body:
Many psychologists doubt such recovered memories. They argue that many are **false memories** created by the **suggestions of therapists**, especially when techniques like repeated questioning, guided imagery or hypnosis are used.

You already know why this is plausible: memory is reconstructive, and misinformation can plant details. **Loftus and Pickrell (1995)** showed that a fair number of adults could be led to 'remember' being lost in a shopping mall as a child, an event that never happened.

slides.heading: A worrying therapy session
slides.story: Adaeze, 28, sees a counsellor in Abuja about low mood. The counsellor says her symptoms 'look like' hidden childhood abuse and asks her each week to imagine what might have happened. After months of this, Adaeze has vivid images of an uncle hurting her. Her family is torn apart. No other evidence exists, and the images first appeared only during the sessions.
slides.takeaway: Repeated suggestion and imagination can build a memory that feels real but may be false.

left.title: Supporters of recovery
points: Trauma can be repressed or dissociated

right.title: Sceptics
points: Feelings and symptoms are not proof

slides.question: The main criticism sceptics make of 'recovered' memories of abuse is that they:
options: Are always deliberate lies
Can never be about real events
May be false memories produced by therapist suggestion
Are stored in sensory memory only
slides.why: Sceptics argue suggestion can create sincere but false memories. They do not claim every such memory is a lie or that real abuse never happens.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect the definition of repression with the word 'unconscious', the Bass and Davis book, and the sceptics' argument. The trap is taking sides crudely. A good answer accepts that abuse is real and serious, while explaining why memories recovered through suggestion need independent support.
slides.sampleQuestion: Critically examine the claim that repressed memories of childhood abuse can be accurately recovered in therapy.
slides.howToAnswer: Define repression and recovered memory, describe the Bass and Davis position, then use reconstructive memory and false-memory research (Loftus) to argue that suggestion can create convincing false memories.

points: Repression: painful material unconsciously pushed out of awareness.
Recovered memory: trauma said to return years later, often in harmless settings.
The Courage to Heal (1988) told readers feelings were enough, without proof.
Sceptics: many recovered memories may be false, planted by suggestion.
Reconstructive memory makes such false memories plausible.

questions.stem: Repression, as a memory process, is best described as:
options: Deliberately refusing to talk about an event
Unconsciously pushing a painful memory out of awareness
Gradual fading of memories through disuse
Losing memories because of a head injury
questions.explanation: Repression is unconscious and is triggered by painful content. Deliberate avoidance is suppression, and fading through disuse is decay.

questions.stem: The book The Courage to Heal (1988), which shaped beliefs about repressed abuse memories, was written by:
options: Elizabeth Loftus and Katherine Ketcham
Brown and Kulik
Ellen Bass and Laura Davis
Stafford and Lynn
questions.explanation: Bass and Davis wrote the book. Stafford and Lynn (2002) wrote about public belief in repressed memories, a nearby name students mix up.

questions.stem: Many psychologists are sceptical of 'recovered' memories mainly because they believe such memories:
options: Are too painful to discuss
Are always about trivial events
Are stored only in the brainstem
May be false memories created by suggestion
questions.explanation: The core worry is that therapists' suggestions can create memories that feel real but are false. The other options are not claims sceptics make.

questions.stem: According to the repressed memory account, a trauma too severe to keep in conscious memory is removed by:
options: Repression, dissociation or both
Rehearsal and consolidation
Chunking and encoding
Decay and displacement
questions.explanation: The account says repression, dissociation or a combination remove the trauma from awareness. Rehearsal and consolidation strengthen memories rather than remove them.

questions.stem: Which of these was a central message of Bass and Davis to readers with no memory of abuse?
options: Seek independent evidence before drawing any conclusion
A feeling that abuse happened, plus symptoms, means it probably did
Only memories recovered under hypnosis can be trusted
Childhood memories cannot be forgotten
questions.explanation: They told readers that a feeling and symptoms were enough and that proof was not their responsibility. Seeking evidence is the sceptics' position, not theirs.

questions.stem: According to the repressed memory view, a recovered memory typically returns:
options: Immediately after the trauma
Only during brain surgery
Later, often in ordinary, harmless circumstances
Never, because repression is permanent
questions.explanation: The account holds that the memory may resurface years later, often triggered in an innocuous setting. Brain surgery is linked to Penfield's flashbacks, not recovered memories.

questions.stem: Ope tells a friend, 'I have been trying hard not to think about my failed exam all week.' A student who calls this repression has confused it with:
options: Dissociation, because Ope has split from reality
Suppression, because Ope is avoiding the thought deliberately
Flashbulb memory, because the event was emotional
Eidetic imagery, because the memory is vivid
questions.explanation: Deliberate avoidance is suppression; repression happens without awareness. Ope is fully aware of the memory, so it is not repressed.

questions.stem: A counsellor tells a client with low mood that her symptoms suggest hidden abuse and asks her to imagine it weekly. Months later she 'remembers' abuse. A memory researcher would be most concerned that:
options: Repeated suggestion and imagination may have created a false memory
The client has developed eidetic imagery
The memory is certainly accurate because it is vivid
The client is deliberately lying for attention
questions.explanation: Suggestion plus repeated imagining is exactly how false memories can be built. Vividness does not prove accuracy, and the client may be entirely sincere.

questions.stem: Which research finding gives sceptics the strongest support when they question recovered memories?
options: Flashbulb memories rank high in emotion and rehearsal
About 5% of children show eidetic imagery
Short-term memory holds about seven items
Adults can be led to recall childhood events that never happened
questions.explanation: Studies such as Loftus and Pickrell's 'lost in the mall' show false childhood memories can be implanted. The other findings are real but irrelevant to the debate.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of the repressed memory controversy EXCEPT:
options: Popular media helped spread belief in repressed memories
Bass and Davis said victims need not prove abuse
Sceptics deny that childhood abuse ever occurs
Some therapists used The Courage to Heal as a key text
questions.explanation: Sceptics question whether memories recovered by suggestion are accurate; they do not deny that abuse happens. The other statements are accurate.

questions.stem: The weakness in the claim 'if your life shows the symptoms, then you were abused' is that:
options: The symptoms listed are common and could have many other causes
Symptoms never appear in abuse survivors
Only children can show symptoms of abuse
Symptoms can be measured only by brain scans
questions.explanation: Low mood, anxiety and similar problems have many possible causes, so they cannot prove a specific past event. Survivors may show such symptoms, but symptoms alone are not proof.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Stafford & Lynn (2002) – wrote The Courage to Heal
Freud – repression as an unconscious defence
Bass & Davis (1988) – implanted false childhood memories
Loftus – argued feelings alone prove abuse
questions.explanation: Freud introduced repression as a defence mechanism. The other pairs are scrambled: Bass and Davis wrote the book, and Loftus is a leading sceptic.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Repression is a conscious decision to forget. II. Recovered memories may return in harmless settings. III. Sceptics argue therapist suggestion can create false memories. IV. Bass and Davis required proof before concluding abuse occurred. Which are correct?
options: I and IV only
II and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
questions.explanation: Statements II and III are correct. Repression is unconscious (I is false), and Bass and Davis explicitly said proof was not needed (IV is false).

questions.stem: A court must decide whether to accept a memory of abuse recovered after two years of suggestive therapy, with no other evidence. Drawing on memory research, the soundest position is that the memory:
options: Must be true, because repressed memories are stored perfectly
Must be false, because abuse is rarely forgotten
Should be accepted if the witness is confident
May be sincere but needs independent corroboration because suggestion can create false memories
questions.explanation: Reconstructive memory means sincere, vivid recall can still be false, especially after suggestion, so corroboration is needed. Confidence is a poor guide, and declaring it certainly false goes beyond the evidence.

questions.stem: Which combination of ideas from earlier sessions best explains how a recovered memory could feel real yet be false?
options: Memory is reconstructive, and post-event suggestion can be blended into memory
Memory is a recorder, and stress improves peripheral details
Sensory memory is large, and short-term memory lasts years
Schemas never affect recall, and confidence equals accuracy
questions.explanation: Reconstruction fills gaps and the misinformation effect inserts suggested content, producing a memory that feels genuine. The other combinations contain false claims, such as the recorder view.

lesson.title: Vivid memories and 'photographic' ones
lesson.hook: Where were you when you heard about the shootings at the Lekki toll gate in October 2020? Many Nigerians can name the room, the phone and the person who told them. But are those memories as accurate as they feel?

slides.heading: Flashbulb memories
slides.body:
**Brown and Kulik (1977)** coined the term **flashbulb memory** for an extremely vivid, long-lasting memory of the moment you learned about a shocking, surprising or highly emotional event. It feels as if a camera flash froze the scene.

Their famous example was the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy in 1963. People remembered exactly where they were when they heard. Personal events count too, such as hearing of a loved one's death.

slides.heading: What makes a flashbulb
slides.body:
Brown and Kulik named three qualities that turn an ordinary memory into a flashbulb memory.

The event must cause **high surprise**. It must be **important**, with real consequences (**consequentiality**). And it must stir a **strong emotional response**.

Of these, surprise and consequentiality are usually seen as the main determinants, with emotional arousal also playing a part.

terms.meaning: Where you were when you heard.
What you were doing at that moment.
Who or what told you the news.
How the people around you reacted.

slides.question: Tunde remembers that his roommate burst in shouting the news. In Brown and Kulik's scheme, the roommate is the:
options: Aftermath
Other affect
Informant
Ongoing activity
slides.why: The informant is the source of the news. 'Other affect' would be how the roommate felt, not the fact that he delivered the news.

slides.heading: Pillemer: not a special system
slides.body:
**Pillemer (1990)** argued flashbulb memories are not a separate *kind* of memory. Every memory varies along three dimensions: **emotion**, **consequentiality** and **rehearsal** (how often you think or talk about the event afterwards).

Flashbulb memories simply score **high on all three**, which is why they are so memorable. Notice that rehearsal matters: you have probably retold your Lekki story many times.

slides.heading: Vivid but not accurate
slides.body:
Flashbulb memories **feel** certain, but **Curci and colleagues (2001)** found they fade at roughly the **same speed**, and distort in similar ways, as everyday memories.

A well-known study by **Neisser and Harsch (1992)** asked students the day after the 1986 Challenger space shuttle disaster how they heard the news, then asked again about two and a half years later. Many later accounts differed sharply from the originals, yet people were confident in them. What stays strong is the **confidence**, not the accuracy.

slides.heading: Two versions of one night
slides.story: The night of the Lekki shootings, Halima wrote in her diary that she heard the news from a Twitter live stream in her hostel. Three years later she tells friends, with total certainty, that her mother phoned her at home with the news. When she finds the diary, she is stunned. Both versions felt equally real to her.
slides.takeaway: Flashbulb memories stay vivid and confident, but their details drift like any other memory.

slides.question: Curci and colleagues (2001) found that flashbulb memories:
options: Never fade at all
Fade at about the same rate as ordinary memories
Are stored in sensory memory
Occur only for public events
slides.why: Their vividness is misleading; they are forgotten much like other memories. They can also be about personal events, such as a family death.

slides.heading: Eidetic imagery
slides.body:
A truly **photographic memory**, capturing every detail perfectly and for ever, is doubted by psychologists except perhaps in a few rare cases.

The closest real phenomenon is **eidetic imagery**: holding an image in such detail and clarity that it is almost as if you were still looking at it. **Haber (1980)** reported that about **5% of children** show it. They can keep a picture in view in their mind for **several minutes** after it is removed and answer questions about it.

slides.heading: Limits of eidetic imagery
slides.body:
Eidetic imagery is not perfect. It can include **distortions and additions**, much like episodic memory, and **talking** (vocalising) while holding the image interferes with it.

Eidetic children generally have **no better long-term memory** than their classmates, and almost all of them **lose** the ability before adulthood. A rare exception was **Elizabeth**, an artist and teacher studied by **Stromeyer (1970)**, who could reproduce a poem in a foreign language years later, writing it from the bottom line upwards.

steps.title: Stare
steps.detail: The child looks at a first picture for about 30 seconds.

steps.title: Wait
steps.detail: The picture is removed for a few minutes.

steps.title: Second drawing
steps.detail: A different drawing is shown that looks meaningless alone.

steps.title: Fusion
steps.detail: An eidetic child mentally combines both pictures and reports seeing a face.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: SAQ 10.1 asks for the characteristics of flashbulb memory, so learn the six features and the three qualities. Expect attribution questions (Brown and Kulik, Pillemer, Haber) and traps like 'flashbulb memories are perfectly accurate' or 'eidetic children have superior long-term memory'. Both are false.
slides.sampleQuestion: Explain the characteristics of flashbulb memory and evaluate the claim that such memories are especially accurate.
slides.howToAnswer: Define flashbulb memory (Brown and Kulik, 1977), list the six features and three qualities, add Pillemer's dimensions, then use Curci et al. (2001) and Neisser and Harsch (1992) to show they are vivid and confident but not especially accurate.

points: Flashbulb memory: vivid memory of learning shocking news (Brown & Kulik, 1977).
Six features: place, activity, informant, own affect, other affect, aftermath.
Pillemer: high emotion, consequentiality and rehearsal, not a special system.
Flashbulb memories fade like others; confidence stays high.
Eidetic imagery: about 5% of children, usually lost by adulthood.

questions.stem: The term 'flashbulb memory' was introduced by:
options: Brown and Kulik
Bass and Davis
Neisser and Harsch
Roediger and McDermott
questions.explanation: Brown and Kulik (1977) coined the term. Neisser and Harsch later tested how accurate such memories are, a common mix-up.

questions.stem: Eidetic imagery is best described as the ability to:
options: Recall the moment one heard shocking news
Hold an image so clearly it seems still to be seen
Forget painful memories unconsciously
Remember lists by grouping items
questions.explanation: Eidetic imagery is retaining a picture with near-perceptual clarity. Recalling where one heard shocking news is a flashbulb memory.

questions.stem: According to Haber (1980), roughly what proportion of children show eidetic imagery?
options: About 50%
About 15%
About 5%
Almost all
questions.explanation: About 5% of children show it. 15% is Egeth's cross-race figure from the eyewitness session.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of Brown and Kulik's three qualities that turn a memory into a flashbulb memory?
options: High surprise
Significant importance
Heightened emotion
Repeated exposure to a picture
questions.explanation: The three are surprise, importance and emotional response. Repeated picture exposure has nothing to do with flashbulb memory.

questions.stem: Pillemer (1990) argued that flashbulb memories are:
options: Ordinary memories that score high on emotion, consequentiality and rehearsal
A completely separate memory system
Always perfectly accurate records
Found only in children
questions.explanation: Pillemer denied they form a special system; they are extreme on dimensions all memories share. Brown and Kulik leaned towards a special mechanism.

questions.stem: What usually happens to eidetic imagery as children grow up?
options: It becomes stronger with age
It turns into flashbulb memory
It is almost always lost before adulthood
It spreads to all the senses
questions.explanation: Virtually all eidetic children lose the ability before adulthood. Rare adults like Elizabeth are exceptions.

questions.stem: Ngozi recalls that when she heard of her grandfather's death, everyone in the room began to cry. In Brown and Kulik's six features, this detail is:
options: Own affect
Informant
Place
Other affect
questions.explanation: Others' reactions are 'other affect'. Ngozi's own feelings would be 'own affect', the closest wrong option.

questions.stem: A student has talked about the day of a national tragedy with friends dozens of times. In Pillemer's terms, this repeated talking raises the memory's:
options: Consequentiality
Rehearsal
Surprise
Eidetic quality
questions.explanation: Thinking or talking about an event afterwards is rehearsal. Consequentiality concerns how important the event's consequences are.

questions.stem: In a test, a child stares at one picture for 30 seconds, then later sees a second meaningless drawing and reports seeing a face. This shows that the child:
options: Retained an eidetic image and fused it with the second drawing
Has a flashbulb memory of the first picture
Has repressed the first picture
Has superior long-term memory for faces
questions.explanation: The face appears only if the first image is held and combined with the second. Eidetic children do not have better long-term memory, so that option is a trap.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of eidetic imagery EXCEPT:
options: It is subject to distortions and additions
Talking while holding the image interferes with it
It can last for several minutes after a picture is removed
Eidetic children have much better long-term memory than peers
questions.explanation: Eidetic children generally have no better long-term memory than others. The other three statements are all accurate.

questions.stem: The finding of Curci and colleagues (2001) that flashbulb memories are forgotten like other memories most directly challenges the view that:
options: Flashbulb memories involve emotion
Flashbulb memories are a special, fixed record
Flashbulb memories can concern personal events
People rehearse flashbulb memories
questions.explanation: If they fade normally, they are not a permanent snapshot, which undermines the special-mechanism view. Emotion and rehearsal remain part of the account.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Haber (1980) – six features of flashbulb memory
Pillemer (1990) – about 5% of children are eidetic
Stromeyer (1970) – Elizabeth, an adult with eidetic ability
Brown & Kulik (1977) – flashbulb memories fade normally
questions.explanation: Stromeyer studied Elizabeth. Haber reported the 5% figure, Brown and Kulik described the six features, and Curci and colleagues found normal fading.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Flashbulb memories are held with high confidence. II. Flashbulb memories resist forgetting better than all other memories. III. Surprise and consequentiality are key determinants. IV. Pillemer saw rehearsal as one dimension of memorability. Which are correct?
options: I, III and IV only
I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Statements I, III and IV are supported. Statement II is false: Curci and colleagues found they are forgotten at a similar rate to other memories.

questions.stem: In a Neisser-and-Harsch-style study, students describe how they heard shocking news the next day and again years later. The most likely result is that the later accounts:
options: Match the originals exactly, with low confidence
Are forgotten entirely, with no confidence
Become more accurate over time
Often differ from the originals, yet are held with high confidence
questions.explanation: Accounts drift substantially while confidence remains high. That combination is why flashbulb memories are described as vivid but not especially accurate.

questions.stem: A student claims, 'Eidetic imagery is the same as a perfect photographic memory.' Which pair of facts best refutes this?
options: It is found in about 5% of children, and it is triggered by shocking news
It includes distortions and additions, and is usually lost before adulthood
It is caused by therapist suggestion, and it lasts for years
It depends on rehearsal, and it involves six features
questions.explanation: A perfect photographic memory would not distort or fade with age, yet eidetic images do both. Shocking news, six features and rehearsal belong to flashbulb memory.
